title: When Overbuilt Is Just Right for a Vintage Jeep

body_markdown:
Sometime around the turn of the century, when I was in middle school, my friend Bill and I were walking back to my home after a visit to a nearby corner store. We stopped briefly in front of a house with a red pickup in the driveway. The vehicle looked a bit out of the ordinary. A far cry from the everyday models produced by the Big Three, this was no square-body Chevy or Bullnose F-series. Bill turned to me and said, “What do you think this is?” A few thoughts swirled around my adolescent mind. “I think that’s a Jeep,” I said.


A moment later, at the other end of the driveway, a man—well, a high schooler at the time, roughly the size of an oak tree—emerged from beneath the truck’s hood. He quickly clarified that it was, in fact, a Jeep, then folded himself back under the hood, and we wandered on. The man under the hood was Rick, known affectionately by his friends as “Yeti.” The Jeep was his[1963 J300 Gladiator](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/Jeep/Gladiator%20J~300/1963/1963-Jeep-Gladiator%20J~300) , and his garage was a far cry from what it is today. I didn’t know it at the time, but I’d just made a friend for life.


Rick Schmidt


In the small suburb of Broadmoor Village, a funny little slice of unincorporated Daly City, California, Rick’s home falls somewhere between *Leave It To Beaver* and *The Burbs* . The house is fastidiously maintained. The grass is green and always mowed, the plants and shrubs trimmed and tidy. Not a single bit of peeling paint exists. Everything is always in its place. Most of the time, his home looks like another quiet slice of Americana.


Until the barn doors of the garage are opened. (The standard garage door was removed to make room for an overhead crane.)


Rick Schmidt


If you walk by Rick’s house today, you’ll likely hear the howl of an angle grinder emanating through the atmosphere. You might notice the electric blue glow of the welder casting oddly shaped shadows on the neighbors’ houses and detect the faint sounds of heavy metal music when the cutting and grinding are paused. You may think this behavior rude, but if you knew Rick, you’d understand why people happily ignore the brash tones echoing through their little street. Rick is a helper, a teacher to those seeking knowledge, and he’s the kind of guy you want around when the excrement hits the fan.


Rick, his Jeep, and the garage are all products of a lengthy evolution.


The process started when Rick was just a kid. His dad, Jim, owned a small moving company that was based in the same building as a machine shop. When Rick wasn’t in school, he was at work with his dad. His young eyes wandered from the moving business and he was became captivated by the sights and sounds of the machine shop.


Rick Schmidt


Rick Schmidt


“I was just immersed in it from a very young age. Growing up, I got to meet some of the most interesting people that had some pretty unique jobs. I met the guys who were the machinists at the dry dock that taught me how to run a lathe,” Rick says.


Even when you’re 12 years old, working with family is difficult. “I had to learn to fix things myself, because you can’t take everything to a shop. So when my dad fired me for, like, the twelfth time, I ended up getting a job at Daly City Saw and Lawn Mower.”


Rick Schmidt


The owner paid Rick in parts and equipment because of his age, and this led to his first mode of oddball motorized transportation. Some kids had scooters or bikes; Rick cruised around the neighborhood on a ride-on reel mower. Sure, it was more at home on a putting green than a suburban street, but wheels are wheels.


He still helped out his dad when needed, lending a hand repairing the trucks and other equipment. This only furthered his love for diesel engines and heavy machinery. By the time he was about halfway through high school, all that time spent crouched over greasy lawn mower parts and under the hoods of trucks had given him an appetite for a project. He and his dad decided to look for something they could work on together at night when Jim got home from work, as a way to bond over a shared interest.


The Jeep, funnily enough, wasn’t their first choice. They looked at several different trucks—Chevys, Fords, maybe a couple of Dodges—but the deals kept falling apart. When the high school auto shop unloaded some of its fleet in anticipation of a remodel, Rick saw an opportunity.


“The Jeep had been sitting on a lift since the ’80s, and they couldn’t get parts for it because it had a unique engine in it. It actually came with two engines. It had a four-cylinder Perkins diesel, which immediately was out of the question because that thing was just clapped—it was done. It had a blown-out cylinder. The truck also came with a hemi 230 Tornado straight-six. It was really rare for the time. I bought that truck in a box for $750.”


Once the Jeep-in-a-box was home, the fun began.


Rick Schmidt


The first order of business, after assembling the truck, was to get the thing running. The original, 230-cubic-inch inline-six had been off the road for a long time. It did eventually run, but never very well. It got the axe. In its place went another straight-six. This one was a bit more common—an overhead-valve, 232-cu-in AMC unit pulled from[a junkyard Pacer](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/final-parking-space/final-parking-space-1975-amc-pacer-d-l-coupe/) . That engine eventually had enough, too, and took its place in the great junkyard in the sky. Rick and his dad went through four different AMC 258-cu-in inline-sixes before they finally found one that worked properly. Then that one fell victim to a rogue nut that made its way down the carburetor. Finally, Rick decided he’d had enough of inline-sixes.


“We finally settled on a 302 Ford that we got out of a wrecked Crown Victoria cop car,” Rick says. “We later found out it was a full roller motor that somebody turned into a 347 stroker motor.”


Sometimes you get very lucky[at the ol’ pick and pull](https://www.hagerty.com/media/maintenance-and-tech/how-to-build-the-perfect-junkyard-tool-kit/) .


Rick Schmidt


The rest of the J300’s drivetrain went through similar changes. Parts were hard to find for the original, tapered Dana 44 axles, and with the widespread availability of standard Dana 44 units, it only made sense to swap them out. While he was in there, Rick swapped in front and rear leaf springs from a Kaiser M-715, basically a militarized version of the Jeep Gladiator. The axle upgrade proved its worth for a long time, and the truck probably would have remained in that configuration if not for one fateful day when Rick used the Jeep to get a very large forklift unstuck from some railroad tracks. A noble cause, to say the least, but it obliterated the truck’s front axle.


Rather than simply rebuild it, Rick and his dad decided to upgrade. Rick used his connections as a heavy equipment mechanic to source a Dana 60 kingpin front axle assembly from a four-wheel-drive Chevy service truck. He changed out the old 44 rear end for a full-floating Dana 60 and stuffed the axles with 4.10:1 gears. He treated the rear end to a Detroit Locker and installed[a TrueTrac limited-slip](https://www.hagerty.com/media/maintenance-and-tech/welcome-to-diff-world-6-types-of-differentials-and-how-they-work/) to the front. The transmission is a four-speed T-18 with a 6:1 first gear, and a Dana 20 twin-stick transfer case with a 4:1 low gear hangs off the back. The old Jeep is geared low enough to pull any stump imaginable—or pull giant forklifts from train tracks without breaking.


Rick Schmidt


Rick Schmidt


Eventually the front leafs came out in favor of a custom five-link front suspension built by Rick. Heavy-duty rod ends and 2 x .250-inch-wall drawn-over-mandrel (DOM) tubing secure the massive hunk of Dana 60 to the frame. Skyjacker two-inch lift springs from an F-250 (provided by yours truly), with the accompanying shocks, now handle the ride quality.


Rick built a couple of bombproof bumpers for the Jeep as well. The front is home to a twelve-thousand-pound Warn winch, a 60-inch Hi-Lift jack, and a couple of auxiliary lights pulled from a forklift.


Over the 20 or so years Rick was building his Jeep, he also amassed a collection of tools that would make anyone green with envy.


“The garage came out of necessity, ’cause I kept pushing the envelope further and further,” says Rick. “I’m not a guy who really wants to sit down and watch TV for hours on end. I wanna be doing things and be productive. My mindset is: Why am I gonna pay somebody else to build it when I can do it better myself? So I’ve acquired a massive amount of tools over the years.”


Rick Schmidt


Part of the reason for that massive amount of tools is because of the variety of mechanically oriented jobs he’s held: forklift mechanic, general heavy-equipment mechanic, engineer at a brewery in the heart of San Francisco, and damn near anything else you can think of that involves solving mechanical problems. Each job was an opportunity to gather specialized tools, all of which are now carefully arranged in a one-car garage, along with a few other items that you won’t find in the arsenal of an everyday mechanic: an upright Bridgeport milling machine, a lathe, a press brake, welders of almost every type, a plasma cutter, an overhead crane, and a small but mighty Hyster forklift, just to list a few. And yes, you can still move around well enough to grab an ice-cold beverage from the vintage Pepsi machine.


While the garage has likely reached the apex of its evolution, the Jeep is another story. Many people think of California as a state inhabited by mostly rust-free vehicles; however, a life lived anywhere near the coast paints a different picture, especially in the foggy San Francisco Bay Area. Throw in a vehicle already prone to rust, and things go south in a hurry. Rick is currently on the hunt for a rust-free cab, or a cab as rust-free as something made in the 1960s can be. You can bet the Jeep (or the tools) won’t be leaving Rick’s possession anytime soon—at least not while he’s still breathing.
